propositions.text: The Attorney General seeks judicial review of the Appeal Division's decision in Canada Employment Insurance Commission v. Z. E.
propositions.quote: The applicant, the Attorney General of Canada, seeks judicial review of the decision of the Appeal Division of the Social Security Tribunal (SST) in Canada Employment Insurance Commission v. Z. E., 2025 SST 855 (the Decision).

propositions.text: The Appeal Division decided the Commission could not reconsider Ms. Emamifar's parental benefits claim after 36 months unless a false or misleading statement was made.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division decided that the Canada Employment Insurance Commission (Commission) could not reconsider Ms. Zahra Emamifar’s claim for parental benefits under the Employment Insurance Act, S.C. 1996, c. 23 (the Act) more than 36 months after those benefits had last been paid to her.

propositions.text: The Commission may extend reconsideration period to 72 months only if a false or misleading statement was made under subsection 52(5) of the Act.
propositions.quote: The Commission may only extend the reconsideration period beyond 36 months to 72 months where it is of the opinion that a false or misleading statement or representation has been made in connection with the claim: subsection 52(5) of the Act.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division found no evidence Ms. Emamifar made false or misleading statements; her omission to inform was not a statement or representation.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division concluded that this condition had not been met because there was no evidence that the information Ms. Emamifar provided in her application for parental benefits was false or misleading and her failure to inform the Commission that she had returned to work and received earnings was an omission that did not qualify as a statement or representation.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Attorney General seeks judicial review of the Appeal Division's decision that the Commission cannot reconsider benefits after 36 months unless a false statement was made; the Appeal Division found no false statement by Ms. Emamifar.

propositions.text: The Court reviews the Decision for reasonableness, not substituting its own decision for the Appeal Division's.
propositions.quote: In assessing whether the Decision is reasonable, it is not the role of this Court to ask what decision it would have made in place of that made by the Appeal Division.

propositions.text: The Court can set aside the Decision only if it lacks justification, intelligibility, and transparency.
propositions.quote: This Court can set aside the Decision only if the Attorney General establishes that it exhibits shortcomings or flaws sufficiently central or significant such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility, and transparency.

propositions.text: The Attorney General has not met the burden to show the Decision is unreasonable.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, I am of the view that the Attorney General has not met this burden.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains it reviews the Decision for reasonableness and finds the Attorney General has not shown it is unreasonable.

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar applied for maternity and parental benefits effective October 6, 2019, expecting to return to work 18 months later.
propositions.quote: Ms. Emamifar applied for maternity and parental benefits under the Act effective October 6, 2019, indicating on her application that she expected to return to work with her employer 18 months later, on April 3, 2021.

propositions.text: She selected extended parental benefits for 61 weeks at 33% weekly earnings instead of standard benefits for 35 weeks at 55%.
propositions.quote: She selected “extended parental benefits” paid for 61 weeks within an 18-month period at a weekly benefit rate of 33% of her weekly insurable earnings, rather than “standard parental benefits” paid for 35 weeks within a 12-month period at a weekly benefit rate of 55% of her weekly insurable earnings.

propositions.text: Her employer issued a record of employment on October 17, 2019, with expected recall date April 2, 2021, consistent with 18-month absence.
propositions.quote: On October 17, 2019, her employer issued an electronic record of employment (ROE) with April 2, 2021, as her expected date of recall, consistent with an 18-month absence from work.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Emamifar applied for extended parental benefits in October 2019, expecting to return to work after 18 months, with employer's ROE confirming this.

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar sought exemption from biweekly reporting to receive EI benefits, agreeing to an Exemption Declaration.
propositions.quote: Ms. Emamifar also sought to be exempted from reporting every two weeks in order to receive her employment insurance (EI) benefits (the reporting exemption).

propositions.text: The Exemption Declaration required agreement to report work, money received, or situations affecting benefits, and to notify after last payment.
propositions.quote: I understand that I am making a claim for benefits covering every week of my period of eligibility and I accept that I will not be required to complete reports for this period. I also agree to inform Service Canada immediately if, while I am collecting Employment Insurance benefits • I work, • I receive money, or • any situation arises that affects my Employment Insurance benefits. Following receipt of my last payment of benefits, I agree to notify Service Canada to confirm that I have declared any situation or earnings that have the effect of reducing or eliminating my benefits.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes Ms. Emamifar's agreement to an exemption from biweekly reporting with obligations to report work or earnings affecting benefits.

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar selected “yes” to agree to the Exemption Declaration statements.
propositions.quote: Ms. Emamifar selected “yes”, indicating her agreement with the statements set out in the exemption declaration.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Emamifar agreed to the exemption declaration by selecting yes.

propositions.text: The application included a “Rights and Responsibilities” section requiring accurate reporting of employment earnings.
propositions.quote: Another section of the online application, titled “Rights and Responsibilities,” specified, among other things, that “[w]hen requesting maternity or parental benefits, you must… accurately report all employment earnings… in the week(s) in which they were earned” (emphasis in the original).

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar acknowledged reading, understanding, and accepting her rights and responsibilities.
propositions.quote: Ms. Emamifar checked a statement that she had read, understood and accepted her rights and responsibilities.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the application required accurate earnings reporting and Ms. Emamifar accepted these rights and responsibilities.

propositions.text: The application’s Attestation section required declaration that information given was true to the best of knowledge.
propositions.quote: Finally, the “Attestation” section of the online application stated in part: “I declare that the information given to the questions on the Application for Employment Insurance benefits online and questionnaires is true to the best of my knowledge.”

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar accepted the attestation by checking the statement.
propositions.quote: Ms. Emamifar checked a statement that she accepted the attestation.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Emamifar attested that her application information was true to the best of her knowledge.

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar returned to work earlier than expected; employer submitted revised ROE dated October 21, 2020.
propositions.quote: However, Ms. Emamifar returned to work earlier than she had expected. Her employer submitted to Service Canada a revised electronic ROE dated October 21, 2020, indicating that she had returned to work in October 2020.

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar did not inform the Commission of her return to work or earnings and continued receiving benefits until March 27, 2021.
propositions.quote: Ms. Emamifar did not inform the Commission that she had returned to work or was receiving employment income. She continued receiving parental benefits until March 27, 2021.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Emamifar returned to work early in October 2020 but did not inform the Commission and continued receiving benefits until March 2021.

propositions.text: On July 31, 2024, the Commission decided Ms. Emamifar made a false or misleading statement by failing to declare employment income.
propositions.quote: On July 31, 2024, the Commission sent a notice of decision to Ms. Emamifar stating that it was of the opinion that a false or misleading statement or representation had been made because she had failed to declare employment income.

propositions.text: The Commission assessed an overpayment of $8,087 and sent the notice more than 36 months after last benefit payment.
propositions.quote: The Commission decided that these earnings needed to be allocated to her claim and it assessed an overpayment of benefits in the amount of $8,087. Significantly, this notice of decision was sent more than 36 months following the last payment of Ms. Emamifar’s benefits.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Commission found Ms. Emamifar made a false statement by not declaring income, assessed overpayment, and sent notice after 36 months.

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar sought reconsideration, explaining she returned early due to spouse's layoff and misunderstood benefit payments.
propositions.quote: Ms. Emamifar sought reconsideration. She explained to the Commission that she had originally intended to be off work for 18 months, but that she had to return to work after 12 months when her spouse was laid off during the COVID pandemic. She said that she had assumed that she had been approved for a lump sum with the option to have the benefits paid over 12 or 18 months and that she had believed that the continuing benefit payments were normal since she had already been approved for the entire amount of benefits.

propositions.text: She expected her employer to notify the Commission of her return to work.
propositions.quote: She also explained that she had expected her employer to notify the Commission of her return to work.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Emamifar sought reconsideration, explaining early return due to spouse's layoff and expecting employer to notify Commission.

propositions.text: The Commission denied reconsideration and Ms. Emamifar appealed to the General Division of the SST.
propositions.quote: The Commission denied Ms. Emamifar’s request for reconsideration, and she appealed to the General Division of the SST.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Commission denied reconsideration and Ms. Emamifar appealed to the General Division.

propositions.text: The Commission argued to the General Division that Ms. Emamifar's failure to report was an omission constituting a false statement due to her reporting exemption agreement.
propositions.quote: The Commission submitted to the General Division that Ms. Emamifar’s failure to report her return to work and her earnings was an “omission of information” that constituted a false statement because she had agreed to the conditions for securing a reporting exemption in her application for benefits.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Commission argued Ms. Emamifar's omission was a false statement due to her reporting exemption agreement.

propositions.text: The General Division allowed Ms. Emamifar’s appeal, finding the Commission relied on paragraph 38(1)(a) of the Act to reconsider her claim.
propositions.quote: The General Division allowed Ms. Emamifar’s appeal (Z. E. v. Canada Employment Insurance Commission, 2025 SST 856 (GD Decision)). It found that the Commission had relied on paragraph 38(1)(a) of the Act to reconsider her claim.

propositions.text: The Commission did not impose a penalty on Ms. Emamifar, as later recognized by the Appeal Division.
propositions.quote: As the Appeal Division later recognized in the Decision, the Commission did not impose a penalty on Ms. Emamifar.

paragraphs.summary: The General Division allowed Ms. Emamifar’s appeal, finding the Commission relied on paragraph 38(1)(a) but did not impose a penalty.

propositions.text: Under subsections 52(1) and (5), the Commission has 36 months to reconsider claims, or 72 months if a false or misleading statement is made.
propositions.quote: The General Division noted that under subsections 52(1) and (5) of the Act, the Commission has 36 months after benefits have been paid to reconsider a claim, or 72 months if it is of the opinion that a claimant has made a false or misleading statement or representation.

propositions.text: The General Division adopted J. S. reasoning that a representation requires an action, not an omission like failure to report.
propositions.quote: It adopted the reasoning of the Appeal Division in J. S. v. Canada Employment Insurance Commission, 2017 SSTADEI 431 at paragraph 13 [J. S.] that a “representation requires action, whether in verbal, written, visual, or other form”, and does not include an omission, such as a failure to report.

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar made no statements about her return to work because she was exempted from reporting.
propositions.quote: It found that Ms. Emamifar had “made no statements or representations about her return to work and earnings because she was exempted from completing the reports where she would otherwise have done so” (GD Decision at para. 39).

propositions.text: Since no false or misleading statements were made, the Commission had no authority to extend reconsideration beyond 36 months.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the General Division concluded that, since the Commission could not establish that Ms. Emamifar had made false or misleading statements, it had no authority to extend the period to reconsider her claim for benefits.

paragraphs.summary: The General Division found the Commission had no authority to extend reconsideration beyond 36 months because Ms. Emamifar made no false statements, adopting J. S. reasoning.

propositions.text: The Commission appealed the General Division’s decision to the Appeal Division.
propositions.quote: The Commission appealed the General Division’s decision to the Appeal Division.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Commission appealed the General Division’s decision to the Appeal Division.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division agreed the Commission did not impose a penalty and the General Division erred in relying on paragraph 38(1)(a) to extend reconsideration.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division agreed with the Commission that it had not imposed a penalty on Ms. Emamifar, and that the General Division had thus erred in concluding that the Commission had relied on paragraph 38(1)(a) of the Act to extend the period for reconsideration of Ms. Emamifar’s claim to 72 months.

propositions.text: The authority to extend reconsideration beyond 36 months is in subsection 52(5) of the Act, not paragraph 38(1)(a).
propositions.quote: Rather, the authority to extend the reconsideration period beyond 36 months is in subsection 52(5) of the Act.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division substituted its own decision for the General Division's rather than remitting the file back.
propositions.quote: Having found an error of law, the Appeal Division decided to substitute its own decision for that of the General Division rather than sending the file back.

paragraphs.summary: The Appeal Division found the General Division erred relying on paragraph 38(1)(a), held subsection 52(5) governs extension, and substituted its own decision.

propositions.text: The Commission argued Ms. Emamifar agreed to report all earnings and her failure to do so misled the Commission into paying benefits.
propositions.quote: The Commission submitted that Ms. Emamifar had agreed to the responsibilities set out in the online application, including the obligation to report all her earnings in the week they were earned. The Commission further submitted that, because Ms. Emamifar had failed to comply with her reporting obligations when she returned to work early, the Commission had been misled into paying her benefits and it was reasonable for the Commission to come to the opinion that her failure to inform was a false or misleading statement or representation (Decision at para. 38).

paragraphs.summary: The Commission argued Ms. Emamifar's failure to report earnings misled it into paying benefits, constituting a false or misleading statement.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division noted the Commission's faulting Ms. Emamifar for failing to report was describing an omission.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division noted that in faulting Ms. Emamifar for failing to report to the Commission her return to work and her earnings, the Commission was describing an omission.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division decided failure to report (an omission) is not a statement or representation under subsection 52(5).
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division decided that failure to report information (an omission) did not constitute a statement or representation for the purpose of subsection 52(5), based largely on an analysis of the text of subsection 52(5), a comparison of that provision with paragraph 38(1)(a) of the Act, and the reasoning set out in J. S. and in a decision of the General Division in B. S. v. Canada Employment Insurance Commission, 2024 SST 469 [B. S.].

paragraphs.summary: The Appeal Division found that failure to report is an omission and not a statement or representation under subsection 52(5).

propositions.text: The Appeal Division acknowledged Ms. Emamifar attested to responsibilities but found no evidence her application information was false or misleading at the time.
propositions.quote: While the Appeal Division acknowledged that Ms. Emamifar attested to and agreed to the responsibilities set out in the online application, it “[saw] no evidence that the information she provided in her application was false or misleading as it was accurate and truthful at the time she made her application” (Decision at para. 59).

propositions.text: The Appeal Division adopted J. S. interpretation that a representation requires an action, not an omission.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division adopted the interpretation of “representation” in J. S., requiring a verbal, written, visual or other form of action.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division concluded subsection 52(5) does not extend to omissions and Ms. Emamifar made no representation.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, it concluded that subsection 52(5) did not extend to omissions. Considering that Ms. Emamifar was exempt from filing biweekly reports, the Appeal Division found that she had taken no action and thus made no representation. Therefore, it concluded, the Commission could not extend the reconsideration period from 36 to 72 months and reconsider Ms. Emamifar’s claim.

paragraphs.summary: The Appeal Division found Ms. Emamifar's application was truthful, adopted J. S. that representation requires action, and concluded omissions do not extend reconsideration period.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division’s decision is reviewed on a deferential reasonableness standard per Vavilov and Molchan.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division’s decision, including its interpretation of the Act, is reviewable on the deferential standard of reasonableness (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v. Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, [2019] 4 S.C.R. 653 [Vavilov]; Molchan v. Canada (Attorney General), 2024 FCA 46 at para. 10).

propositions.text: Reasonableness requires an internally coherent, rational, justified decision based on facts and law.
propositions.quote: An administrative decision will be reasonable if it is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker (Vavilov at paras. 84‒85; Mason v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2023 SCC 21 at para. 8).

propositions.text: The reviewing court must not substitute its own decision or seek the correct solution.
propositions.quote: Significantly, the reviewing court’s role is not to ask what decision it would have made in the decision maker’s place or to determine the “correct” solution to the problem before the decision maker (Vavilov at para. 83).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the Appeal Division’s decision is reviewed on a deferential reasonableness standard, requiring coherence and justification, without substituting its own decision.

propositions.text: The burden is on the party challenging the decision to show it is unreasonable by demonstrating significant shortcomings or flaws.
propositions.quote: The burden is on the party challenging the decision—in this case, the Attorney General—to show that it is unreasonable by satisfying the reviewing court that there are shortcomings or flaws in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency.

propositions.text: Shortcomings must be central or significant, not superficial or peripheral, to render the decision unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Such shortcomings or flaws cannot be merely superficial or peripheral to the merits of the decision; they must be sufficiently central or significant to render the decision unreasonable (Vavilov at para. 100).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the burden is on the Attorney General to show the decision is unreasonable by significant shortcomings, not superficial flaws.

propositions.text: A reviewing court must examine the decision maker’s reasons respectfully and understand their reasoning process holistically and contextually.
propositions.quote: In evaluating an administrative decision maker’s justification for its decision, a reviewing court must examine the decision maker’s written reasons with respectful attention and seek to understand the reasoning process followed by the decision maker to arrive at its own conclusion (Vavilov at para. 84).

propositions.text: Reasons must not be judged by perfection; lacking all arguments or details is not alone a basis to set aside a decision.
propositions.quote: Reasons must not be assessed against a standard of perfection; the fact they don’t “include all the arguments, statutory provisions, jurisprudence or other details” a reviewing court would prefer is not by itself a sufficient basis for setting aside the decision (Vavilov at para. 91, citing Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses' Union v. Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62, [2011] 3 S.C.R. 708 at para. 16).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains how reviewing courts must respectfully and holistically assess decision reasons without requiring perfection.

propositions.text: The Attorney General submits five shortcomings in the Appeal Division’s reasons that render its decision unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General submits that the Appeal Division’s reasons disclose five shortcomings or flaws that render its decision unreasonable.

propositions.text: The court will address each of the five shortcomings in turn and annex relevant Act provisions.
propositions.quote: I address each of these in turn. For ease of reference, I have annexed the relevant provisions of the Act to these reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Attorney General alleges five shortcomings in the Appeal Division’s reasons and will address them sequentially.

propositions.text: The Attorney General submits the Appeal Division unreasonably concluded that Ms. Emamifar’s application information was not statements or representations.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General submits that the Appeal Division unreasonably concluded that the information, agreements and attestations contained in Ms. Emamifar’s online application for EI benefits were not statements or representations.

paragraphs.summary: The Attorney General argues the Appeal Division wrongly concluded Ms. Emamifar’s application information were not statements or representations.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division considered Ms. Emamifar’s application information to be a statement or representation under subsection 52(5).
propositions.quote: In my view, on a fair reading of the reasons, the Appeal Division considered the information supplied by Ms. Emamifar in her online application, including her responses agreeing to the attestation and statement of responsibilities, to be a statement or representation within the meaning of subsection 52(5), because it turned its mind to whether that information could be false or misleading (Decision at para. 59).

propositions.text: The Appeal Division found no evidence Ms. Emamifar made any statement or representation after filing her application during the reporting exemption period.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division did find that there was “no evidence that [Ms. Emamifar] made any statement or representation to the Commission at all” (Decision at para. 57, emphasis in the original). However, read in context, this can only be understood to refer to the period after she filed her online application during which, due to the reporting exemption, she made no biweekly reports that would have constituted statements or representations.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appeal Division viewed the application info as a statement but found no evidence of statements after application during the reporting exemption.

propositions.text: The Attorney General argues it was unreasonable to find no evidence of false or misleading statements since Ms. Emamifar failed to do what she promised.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General submits that it was unreasonable for the Appeal Division to conclude that it saw “no evidence that the information [Ms. Emamifar] provided in her application was false or misleading as it was accurate and truthful at the time she made her application” (Decision at para. 59).

propositions.text: If a person fails to do what they said they would, that is a reasonable basis to form the opinion of a false or misleading statement.
propositions.quote: In the Attorney General’s view, “if a person says they will do something and then fails to do so, that is a reasonable basis to form the opinion that a false or misleading statement has been made.”

propositions.text: The Appeal Division’s conclusion ignores that Ms. Emamifar continued to receive benefits while working, which supports a false or misleading statement.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the Attorney General argues, it was unreasonable for the Appeal Division to find that Ms. Emamifar’s statements were true and sincere at the time they were made and to ignore that she later failed to do what she said she would do, especially considering that she continued to receive benefits while working.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division’s conclusion means the Commission must prove Ms. Emamifar knew she would not follow through, conflicting with Court decisions that knowledge is not required.
propositions.quote: In the Attorney General’s view, the Appeal Division’s conclusion means that, to establish a false or misleading statement or representation, the Commission would have to prove that Ms. Emamifar knew that she would not follow through on her undertakings when applying for benefits. Such a result would conflict with decisions of this Court that false or misleading statements need not be made knowingly under the reconsideration provision.

paragraphs.summary: The Attorney General argues it was unreasonable to find no false statement since Ms. Emamifar failed to do what she promised, ignoring knowledge is not required.

propositions.text: The Attorney General relies on Dussault, where the Court rejected requiring knowledge to establish false or misleading statements under subsection 52(5).
propositions.quote: As observed by the Attorney General, this Court interpreted the Commission’s authority to extend the period to reconsider a claim for benefits in Canada (Attorney General) v. Dussault, 2003 FCA 372 [Dussault].

propositions.text: Dussault held that subsection 52(5) does not require proof that a false or misleading statement was made knowingly, unlike section 38 which punishes deviant behaviour.
propositions.quote: [11] …[T]here is no connection between [the predecessor to section 38 of the Act], which requires proof that the false statement was made knowingly, and [the predecessor to subsection 52(5)], which contains no such requirement. ... All Parliament requires in s. [52(5)] is that “in the opinion of the Commission, a false or misleading statement… has been made”...

paragraphs.summary: The Attorney General relies on Dussault, which held subsection 52(5) does not require knowledge to establish false or misleading statements.

propositions.text: Reporting exemptions apply only to special benefits, not ordinary EI benefits like in Dussault.
propositions.quote: At the hearing before this Court, counsel for the Attorney General acknowledged that reporting exemptions are only available for special benefits under the Act, such as maternity or parental benefits. The exemptions are not available for ordinary EI benefits, such as those at play in Dussault.

propositions.text: Mr. Dussault was subject to regular biweekly reporting and falsely reported no earnings while receiving self-employed income.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, Mr. Dussault would have been subject to the regular biweekly reporting requirement and would have reported, for each two-week period, that he had not received any earnings, when the evidence before the Commission was that he had received self-employed income.

propositions.text: In Dussault, a false or misleading statement could be objectively inferred from the facts due to the reporting requirement.
propositions.quote: It is in that sense that the existence of a false or misleading statement could be “inferred objectively from the facts.”

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Dussault involved ordinary EI benefits with reporting requirements, allowing objective inference of false statements.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division acknowledged no knowledge requirement under subsection 52(5) and that the Commission must only be of the opinion a false statement was made.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division acknowledged that Dussault had confirmed there is no requirement, under subsection 52(5) of the Act, that a false or misleading statement or representation be made knowingly (Decision at para. 46) and understood that the Commission “only has to be of the opinion that… a false or misleading statement or representation was made” (Decision at para. 45).

propositions.text: The Appeal Division found Ms. Emamifar did not make any false or misleading statements or representations for several reasons.
propositions.quote: It nevertheless found, for the reasons reproduced below, that Ms. Emamifar did not make any false or misleading statements or representations: [54] Generally speaking, when a person applies for benefits and a benefit period is established, they are required to submit biweekly reports. ... [59] I acknowledge that the Claimant attested to and agreed to her responsibilities when she applied for benefits, but I see no evidence that the information she provided in her application was false or misleading as it was accurate and truthful at the time she made her application.

paragraphs.summary: The Appeal Division acknowledged no knowledge requirement but found no false statements by Ms. Emamifar for various reasons.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division distinguished statements in the online application from biweekly report responses.
propositions.quote: It is clear from its reasons that the Appeal Division considered that the statements made by Ms. Emamifar in her online application differed from responses to “specific questions about earnings, availability and other things” posed in typical biweekly reports.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division’s approach aligns with the General Division’s decision in B. S. on similar facts.
propositions.quote: Reading its reasons contextually and in light of prior decisions of the SST (Vavilov at para. 94), I note that the Appeal Division’s approach is consistent with that taken by the General Division in B. S., a case raising similar facts that the Appeal Division referred to in its reasons.

propositions.text: The General Division held a false or misleading statement must come from answering a direct question untruthfully.
propositions.quote: The General Division held that “for an appellant to make a false or misleading statement or representation, it must come from answering a direct question related to their situation in a way that isn’t truthful or accurate” (B. S. at para. 45, emphasis added).

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appeal Division distinguished application statements from biweekly reports, consistent with the General Division in B. S.

propositions.text: Statements in biweekly reports relate to facts at or before the statement time; application statements relate to present intention about future actions.
propositions.quote: According to the Appeal Division (Decision at para. 54) and the General Division (B. S. at para. 45), the statements made by a claimant in response to biweekly reports relate to facts regarding the claimant’s situation at or before the time the statements are made, including whether they are working, have earned income or are available to work. Conversely, both Divisions recognized that the statements in the exemption declaration and rights and responsibilities section of the online application for EI benefits relate to the claimant’s present intention to carry out certain actions in the future (Decision at paras. 56 and 59; B. S. at para. 48).

propositions.text: The timing of agreeing to the exemption declaration is relevant to subsection 52(5) analysis.
propositions.quote: Indeed, in B. S., the General Division observed that “when the [claimant] agreed to the exemption declaration is relevant” to the subsection 52(5) analysis (at para. 48, emphasis in the original).

paragraphs.summary: The Appeal and General Divisions found biweekly reports state facts, while application statements express present intention about future actions.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division viewed Ms. Emamifar’s application statements as present intentions at application time, unlike biweekly report facts.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division’s view that there was no evidence Ms. Emamifar provided false or misleading information in her application must be considered in light of the nature of that information. The information consisted in statements setting out her then (i.e., “at the time she made her application”) present intent to return to work at a specific future date, report future earnings if they occurred and report a return to work in the future.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appeal Division saw Ms. Emamifar’s application statements as present intentions at application time, distinct from biweekly report facts.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division recognized the Commission’s argument that failure to follow through shows false statements but rejected it as conclusive.
propositions.quote: In my view, the Appeal Division’s reasons demonstrate that it grasped the Commission’s argument that Ms. Emamifar’s failure to follow through on her stated intention showed that she had made false or misleading statements (Decision at para. 56).

propositions.text: The Appeal Division concluded failure to carry out intention does not prove the claimant lacked that intention at application time.
propositions.quote: They also show that the Appeal Division concluded that the fact Ms. Emamifar failed to carry out her expressed intention did not, in itself, establish that she did not actually possess that intention at the time she submitted her application.

paragraphs.summary: The Appeal Division understood but rejected that failure to follow through proves lack of intention at application time.

propositions.text: The court disagrees with the Attorney General that the Appeal Division’s decision conflicts with Dussault on intention requirement.
propositions.quote: In light of my previous discussion of Dussault, I disagree with the Attorney General that the Appeal Division’s decision is inconsistent with the Court’s holding that it is unnecessary to find intention when assessing whether a false or misleading statement might exist.

propositions.text: Dussault held that false or misleading statements can be inferred objectively from facts without requiring intention.
propositions.quote: Dussault held that, where a claimant states that he did not receive earnings during a two-week period, the existence of a false or misleading statement is inferred objectively from the facts—in that case, the evidence that he had received amounts over the relevant period.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees that the Appeal Division’s decision conflicts with Dussault, which allows objective inference of false statements without intention.

propositions.text: Langelier involved a claimant attaching a ROE that was alleged false due to lack of proof of payment by Revenue Canada.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General relies on Langelier, where Mr. Langelier attached a ROE alleged false due to Revenue Canada’s decision of no proof of payment.

propositions.text: The Umpire found no proof that the claimant knowingly made false statements in Langelier.
propositions.quote: The Umpire found that, in these circumstances, the Commission had not established that Mr. Langelier had knowingly made false or misleading statements.

paragraphs.summary: Langelier involved a ROE alleged false without proof claimant knowingly made false statements, as found by the Umpire.

propositions.text: The Court held the Umpire erred requiring proof of knowledge but did not err in finding no false statement based on Revenue Canada’s decision alone.
propositions.quote: While this Court held that the Umpire had misdirected himself in requiring that the Commission prove that Mr. Langelier knowingly made false statements, it decided that the Umpire had not erred in finding that it was patently unreasonable for the Commission and Board of Referees to hold that there was a false statement solely based on Revenue Canada’s decision.

propositions.text: A decision based on absence of proof of payment does not alone support a conclusion that no payment was made or that the statement was false.
propositions.quote: [A] decision which, as in the case at bar, is based on the absence of any proof of payment does not by itself support a conclusion that no payment was made and that it is false to say that there was a payment.

paragraphs.summary: The Court held the Umpire erred on knowledge but correctly found no false statement based solely on Revenue Canada’s lack of proof of payment.

propositions.text: Subsection 52(5) is exceptional and strictly construed; the Commission’s burden to claim reimbursement beyond three years is heavy.
propositions.quote: It should be borne in mind that [s. 52(5)] is part of an “exceptional [system], which is a departure from the ordinary law” and must be “strictly construed” (Laforest v. Canada (Attorney General) (1988), 97 N.R. 95 (F.C.A.), per Lacombe J., para. 22). Accordingly, the burden of proof on the Commission when it wishes to go back more than three years to claim reimbursement of an overpayment from a claimant is not a light one.

propositions.text: The Commission cannot rely on vague Revenue Canada decisions without claimant’s knowledge to establish false or misleading statements.
propositions.quote: As indicated by the case at bar, the consequences suffered by a claimant may be significant. In circumstances like these, the Commission cannot simply rely on a Revenue Canada decision rendered without the claimant’s knowledge, based on such a vague allegation as [Translation] “no proof of payment” and giving reasons as brief as they were vague.

paragraphs.summary: Subsection 52(5) is exceptional and strictly construed; the Commission’s burden is heavy and cannot rely on vague Revenue Canada decisions without claimant’s knowledge.

propositions.text: In Dussault, false statements could be objectively inferred from evidence of unreported income; in Langelier, they could not from Revenue Canada’s lack of proof.
propositions.quote: In Dussault, it could be objectively inferred that the claimant had made a false or misleading statement regarding his lack of earnings, because the evidence showed that he was receiving self-employed income at the same time as he declared that he was not. In Langelier, however, the existence of a false or misleading statement could not be objectively inferred from the evidence: Revenue Canada’s inability to find proof that the claimant had been paid, in a proceeding where the claimant could not participate, could not in itself contradict his statement of fact that he had been paid for a week’s work.

propositions.text: The evidence sufficient to form opinion of false or misleading statement varies with circumstances and whether statement is fact or intention.
propositions.quote: It follows that the nature of the evidence that is sufficient to provide the Commission with a reasonable basis to form the opinion that a false or misleading statement or representation has been made may vary with the circumstances, including whether the statement made was one of fact or of intention.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds evidence sufficiency to infer false statements varies by context and whether statement is fact or intention.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division concluded false statements of intention cannot be inferred without evidence claimant lacked that intention at application time.
propositions.quote: In the case at bar, the Appeal Division essentially concluded that the existence of a false or misleading statement could not be objectively inferred from evidence that Ms. Emamifar had not followed through on her stated intention, because that evidence did not contradict the statement made in her application: that her intent at the time she completed the application was to return to work on a certain date, report a return to work and report any earnings.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division found record corroborated Ms. Emamifar’s truthful statement of intention, including employer’s ROE and family circumstances.
propositions.quote: In addition to noting the absence of evidence supporting the existence of a false or misleading statement, the Appeal Division observed that the record corroborated its conclusion that Ms. Emamifar had been truthful when she completed her statement of intention: consistent with that statement, her employer had issued a ROE with April 2, 2021, as her expected date of recall. I note also that the record discloses that Ms. Emamifar’s family faced an unexpected circumstance when her spouse was laid off during the COVID pandemic, prompting her premature return to work.

propositions.text: The court finds nothing unreasonable in the Appeal Division’s conclusion that failure to carry out intention does not prove lack of intention at application time.
propositions.quote: I therefore find nothing unreasonable in the Appeal Division’s conclusion that the fact Ms. Emamifar failed to carry through on her stated intention to return to work or to report earnings was not evidence that she did not in fact hold that intention when she stated it.

paragraphs.summary: The Appeal Division found no evidence Ms. Emamifar lacked intention at application time; the court finds this reasonable.

propositions.text: The Attorney General argues the Appeal Division unreasonably applied the implied exclusion rule in interpreting subsection 52(5).
propositions.quote: The Attorney General argues that the Appeal Division’s interpretation of subsection 52(5) was unreasonable because it was improperly founded on the application of the implied exclusion rule of statutory interpretation.

propositions.text: Reliance on the implied exclusion rule leads to an interpretation inconsistent with the Act’s purpose and allows Ms. Emamifar to keep benefits she is not entitled to.
propositions.quote: Reliance on that rule is improper, the Attorney General submits, because it leads to an interpretation that is inconsistent with the purpose of the Act to pay benefits to claimants who are involuntarily unemployed, and because it works an injustice by allowing Ms. Emamifar to keep benefits to which she is not entitled.

paragraphs.summary: The Attorney General argues the Appeal Division unreasonably relied on the implied exclusion rule, leading to inconsistent and unjust results.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division applied the implied exclusion rule regarding omission in subsection 52(5) of the Act.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Attorney General that the Appeal Division did apply the implied exclusion rule when it noted that, unlike paragraph 38(1)(a) of the Act, subsection 52(5) does not use the word “omission”

propositions.text: The Appeal Division's reliance on implied exclusion was not improper in this case.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded that the Appeal Division’s reliance on implied exclusion was improper in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees the Appeal Division applied the implied exclusion rule but finds its reliance on it was not improper.

propositions.text: Implied exclusion is textual and cannot be the sole basis for statutory interpretation; words must be considered with purpose and scheme.
propositions.quote: The Supreme Court has confirmed that an argument based on implied exclusion is “purely textual in nature and cannot be the sole basis for interpreting a statute … [as the] words of the statute must be considered in conjunction with its purpose and its scheme”

propositions.text: The Appeal Division did not rely solely on implied exclusion but also on SST decisions about the meaning of 'representation'.
propositions.quote: Here, implied exclusion was not the “sole basis” for the Appeal Division’s interpretation of subsection 52(5). The Appeal Division also referred to SST decisions

propositions.text: SST decisions held that a representation requires action and does not include omissions or failure to report information.
propositions.quote: Those decisions held that a representation required action, whether in verbal, written, visual or other form and did not include omissions (J. S. at para. 13) or a failure to report information (B. S. at para. 36).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains implied exclusion cannot be sole basis; Appeal Division also relied on SST decisions defining 'representation' as requiring action, excluding omissions.

propositions.text: The Attorney General did not show the Appeal Division ignored or contradicted the Act's purpose or subsection 52(5).
propositions.quote: Moreover, the Attorney General has not convinced me that the Appeal Division arrived at an interpretation that ignores or is clearly inconsistent with the purpose of the Act or of subsection 52(5).

propositions.text: The Appeal Division relied on prior Court decisions about the purpose and operation of section 52, emphasizing discretion and time limits.
propositions.quote: At paragraph 48 of the Decision, the Appeal Division relies on decisions of this Court which dealt with the purpose and operation of another predecessor to section 52 of the Act, noting: The Commission has the statutory authority under s.52(5) to retroactively determine that benefits have been improperly paid and to ask for repayment.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Attorney General failed to prove the Appeal Division ignored the Act's purpose, noting its reliance on prior Court decisions about section 52.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division understood the Act's purpose and time limits related to reconsidering claims and false or misleading representations.
propositions.quote: In light of this passage and the decisions of this Court that it relied on, I have no doubt that, in interpreting the words “false and misleading statement or representation”, the Appeal Division was aware (1) that the Act aims to provide benefits to claimants who are entitled to these benefits, but also that the power to reconsider claims for benefits was to be “kept strictly within the limits and requirements specified by the Act

propositions.text: If a decision ignores a key element of the Act's purpose that could change the result, failure to consider it is indefensible and unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Had the Attorney General established that, in the Decision, the Appeal Division ignored a key element of the purpose of the Act or of subsection 52(5) that, if considered, may have led it to a different result, the Appeal Division’s failure to consider that element would be indefensible and unreasonable (Vavilov at para. 122).

propositions.text: The Attorney General argues the Appeal Division ignored a key element of the Act's purpose in its interpretation.
propositions.quote: Had the Attorney General established that, in the Decision, the Appeal Division ignored a key element of the purpose of the Act or of subsection 52(5) that, if considered, may have led it to a different result

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appeal Division understood the Act's purpose and time limits; the Attorney General failed to show it ignored key elements.

propositions.text: The Attorney General argues the Appeal Division failed to apply the correct standard under subsection 52(5) regarding reasonable basis for false or misleading statements.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General argues that the Decision is unreasonable because the Appeal Division never asked nor answered the question mandated by subsection 52(5) and this Court’s decisions in Langelier and Dussault: whether the Commission had a reasonable basis to form the opinion that false or misleading statements or representations were made in connection with Ms. Emamifar’s claim.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division considered only whether a false or misleading statement existed, not whether there was a reasonable basis for that opinion.
propositions.quote: Instead, the Attorney General contends, the Appeal Division considered whether a false or misleading statement or representation existed.

paragraphs.summary: The Attorney General argues the Appeal Division failed to apply the correct standard under subsection 52(5) about reasonable basis for false or misleading statements.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division summarized the Commission’s submissions and set out the appropriate standard under subsection 52(5).
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division accurately summarized the Commission’s submissions on the appropriate standard to apply under subsection 52(5) in its reasons (Decision at para. 38) and at the hearing before it.

propositions.text: Although the Appeal Division did not expressly state it found no reasonable basis for the Commission's opinion, its findings imply that conclusion.
propositions.quote: It would no doubt have been preferable for the Appeal Division to expressly state that it found no reasonable basis on which the Commission could form the opinion that Ms. Emamifar made a false or misleading statement in relation to her claim.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division found no evidence Ms. Emamifar made false or misleading statements or representations.
propositions.quote: given its findings that there was no evidence the information Ms. Emamifar provided in her online application was false or misleading and no evidence in the record she made other statements or representations.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appeal Division applied the correct standard and implicitly found no reasonable basis for false or misleading statements by Ms. Emamifar.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division agreed with the General Division's reasoning in B. S., which relied on CUB decisions.
propositions.quote: the Appeal Division expressed its agreement with the reasoning set out by the General Division in B. S. which, in turn had relied on Canadian Umpire Benefit (CUB) decisions

propositions.text: The Attorney General argues B. S. and CUB decisions were irrelevant because they involved penalties not imposed on Ms. Emamifar.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General submits that B. S. and these CUB decisions were irrelevant because they involved circumstances in which the Commission had assessed penalties against the claimant for making false statements or representations under section 38 of the Act. Since penalties were not imposed on Ms. Emamifar, the Attorney General submits it was unreasonable for the Appeal Division to rely on B. S. and, indirectly, on the CUB decisions

paragraphs.summary: The Appeal Division relied on General Division and CUB decisions; the Attorney General argues these were irrelevant due to lack of penalties on Ms. Emamifar.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division's reliance on B. S. and CUB decisions was reasonable as they concluded failure to submit reports is not a statement or representation.
propositions.quote: In B. S., the General Division relied on the CUB decisions to conclude that the failure to submit reports cannot be considered “a statement or representation” and, therefore, a false or misleading statement or representation. It is not unreasonable for the Appeal Division to adopt the reasoning of the General Division in interpreting the meaning of these terms.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appeal Division reasonably relied on B. S. and CUB decisions interpreting failure to submit reports as not a statement or representation.

propositions.text: The party challenging a decision must show central or significant flaws to prove unreasonableness.
propositions.quote: As the party challenging the Decision, the Attorney General bore the burden to show that it was unreasonable by identifying sufficiently central or significant shortcomings or flaws in the Decision

propositions.text: The Attorney General failed to meet the burden to show the Decision was unreasonable.
propositions.quote: In my view, for the foregoing reasons, the Attorney General has failed to meet its burden.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Attorney General bore the burden to show unreasonableness but failed to do so.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss this application for judicial review.

propositions.text: No costs are ordered as Ms. Emamifar did not participate in the proceedings.
propositions.quote: Since Ms. Emamifar did not participate in the proceedings, I would not order costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the judicial review application and declines to order costs due to non-participation by Ms. Emamifar.
